title: Strong Bitter Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: Strong bitter, or ESB, is the biggest beer in the English bitter family. Learn its numbers, history and how to taste it.
teaser: The top rung of the English bitter ladder. Strong bitter is fuller, maltier and still built for the pub.
standfirst: Strong bitter is the most robust member of the English bitter family, often sold as ESB. It is maltier and stronger than an ordinary bitter while keeping the same balance of malt and English hops. Here is what defines it.
sections: The top of the bitter ladder

English bitter comes in three broad strengths. Ordinary bitter is the lightest, around 3.2 to 3.8% ABV. Best bitter sits in the middle, around 3.8 to 4.6%. Strong bitter is the biggest, which the BJCP places at roughly 4.6 to 6.2% ABV with bitterness of around 30 to 50 IBU.

All three share the same idea: a balance of malt and hops in a beer designed for the pub. Strong bitter simply turns the volume up. Our guide to English bitter covers the whole family.
Where the name ESB comes from

Many people call strong bitter ESB, short for Extra Special Bitter. The name comes from a famous beer brewed by Fuller's in London, which has used it for decades. Because that beer became so well known, ESB became shorthand for the style, especially in the United States.

In Britain, brewers tend to sell strong bitters under their own names rather than calling them ESB. In the BJCP guidelines the category is formally Strong Bitter, with ESB mentioned as a common name. If you see ESB on a menu, expect a strong bitter, though American versions can be much hoppier than English ones.

A strong bitter starts with English pale ale malt and usually some crystal malt for caramel and colour. The colour runs from deep gold to copper. Malt flavour is rich: biscuit, toast, caramel and sometimes a light dried fruit note.

The hops are typically English varieties such as East Kent Goldings or Fuggle. They give earthy, floral, woody and gently spicy notes rather than the citrus of American hops. The bitterness is firm but balanced by the malt. The beer should finish moderately dry, inviting another sip rather than leaving you thirsty.
Burton water and the mineral edge

Many classic English pale ales and bitters owe their character to water. Burton upon Trent, an English brewing town, has very hard water rich in calcium sulphate, also called gypsum. Sulphate makes hop bitterness feel crisp and dry. Brewers elsewhere began adding gypsum to their own water to copy it, a practice known as Burtonisation.

That matters for Indian brewers, whose water ranges from soft municipal supply to very hard borewell water. A strong bitter brewed with soft water can taste flabby. One brewed with too much sulphate can taste harsh. Testing the water and adjusting calcium and sulphate is basic good practice for the style.

Yeast matters too. English ale strains usually leave some fruity esters, often described as pear, apple or marmalade, which add depth to a strong bitter. They tend to ferment around 18 to 20 °C and many flocculate well, dropping bright in the cask. Some English strains also leave a faint trace of diacetyl, which a few drinkers accept in small amounts. A strong buttery note, though, is a fault.

In Britain, strong bitter is often served from the cask at cellar temperature, around 11 to 13 °C, with gentle carbonation. That service lets the malt and hop aromas show. A pint poured ice cold and fizzy loses much of its character.

In India, cask ale is rare, so most strong bitters are kegged. Asking the bar to serve it slightly warmer than a lager, closer to 8 to 10 °C, helps. Lower carbonation helps too. A bitter should feel smooth and rounded rather than sharply fizzy.

Strong bitter has enough malt to stand up to rich food and enough bitterness to cut fat. It works with a mutton curry, a beef fry from Kerala or a plate of fish and chips. Caramel and toast flavours from the malt pick up the browning on roast and fried food.

At 5 to 6% ABV it is stronger than a standard pint of lager in Britain, though close to many Indian strong lagers. Pace yourself, drink water and never drive after drinking. Our guide to brewing an English bitter at home covers a lighter, easier-drinking version.

Strong bitter is a lesson in balance. Judging it means asking whether the malt supports the hops or the hops overwhelm the malt. It also means asking whether the finish is clean or cloying. These are questions that trained tasters ask of every beer. They are easier to learn with guidance and good examples.

For a first step, pour a best bitter and a strong bitter side by side. Taste the best bitter first. Note how the extra malt in the strong bitter changes the body, colour and the way the bitterness lands. You will see how balance shifts as strength goes up.
faqs: What is the difference between bitter and ESB?
ESB is a common name for strong bitter, the strongest of the English bitter family, at roughly 4.6 to 6.2% ABV.
The name comes from Extra Special Bitter, a famous beer from Fuller's of London, which became shorthand for the style.
What hops are used in strong bitter?
Usually English varieties such as East Kent Goldings and Fuggle, which give earthy, floral and woody notes.
How should strong bitter be served?
Ideally from the cask at around 11 to 13 °C with gentle carbonation, or from keg slightly warmer than lager.
